explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Verse 12 says they bound themselves with an oath not to eat or drink until they had killed Paul. I think this is a heavy part of the story. Their oath is tied to eating and drinking.

Sleep never comes up in this oath. Verse 12 says they swore not to eat or drink until they had killed Paul. Nobody in the text swears off a nap, so the pillows stay safe. The oath is about food and drink.
Close, but work and travel aren't in the oath. Verse 12 says they bound themselves not to eat or drink until they had killed Paul. Only eating and drinking are named in it.
That's it, baker. Verse 13 says more than forty of them were involved in this plot. More than forty means the number was bigger than forty. That's a whole lot of men for one plan.

Twelve is too small for this crew. Verse 13 says more than forty men were involved in the plot. I'd say twelve would still be plenty of trouble, but the text counts higher. Forty-plus is the number to hold onto.

Ninety isn't the number the text gives. Verse 13 says more than forty of them were involved in the plot. The text doesn't give a count beyond that, so I can't tell you ninety. Forty is the number in the verse.

explanations.answer: Ask the commander to bring Paul down
explanations.explanation: Right on target. In verses 14 and 15 the plotters go to the chief priests and elders and tell them to have the Sanhedrin petition the commander to bring Paul down. The Sanhedrin is the Jewish council. The whole plan hangs on that one request.

explanations.answer: Ask the commander to set Paul free
explanations.explanation: Freedom isn't the favor they want. They've sworn an oath not to eat or drink until they've killed Paul (Acts 23:12). In verse 15 they ask the Sanhedrin to petition the commander to bring him down. Letting Paul go would wreck their whole plot.

explanations.answer: Ask the governor to hear Paul's case
explanations.explanation: The governor isn't part of their request. In verses 14 and 15 they go to the chief priests and elders and ask for a petition to the commander to bring Paul down. The governor, Felix, shows up later in the story, and that's the commander's doing. The plotters only want Paul brought down to them.
Yes, friend. Verse 15 says the request is to be made on the pretext of examining his case more carefully. A pretext is a cover story. Right after that they say, “We are ready to kill him on the way.”

This one's True. Verse 15 says the Sanhedrin is to petition the commander on the pretext of examining Paul's case more carefully. A pretext is a cover story. The plotters want the request to sound like an honest question while they wait to kill him on the way.
You got it, baker. In verse 15 the plotters say, "We are ready to kill him on the way." The way means the trip as Paul is brought down to the Sanhedrin. They plan to ambush him along the road.
The barracks isn't the plan. Paul is held there, but verse 15 says, "We are ready to kill him on the way." The plan only works if the commander brings Paul out. That's why they want him brought down.

The temple gate never comes up. Verse 15 says the plotters are ready to kill him on the way, meaning while Paul is being brought down. The text puts the ambush on the trip itself. No gate is mentioned.

explanations.answer: Goes into the barracks and tells Paul
explanations.explanation: That's the one. Verse 16 says Paul's nephew, his sister's son, heard about the plot, went into the barracks and told Paul. He walked right in with the news. Good thing somebody did.

explanations.answer: Goes to the chief priests and pleads
explanations.explanation: He doesn't go to the chief priests. They're the ones the plotters went to with the plan (Acts 23:14). Verse 16 says Paul's nephew went into the barracks and told Paul. He took the news to the man in danger.
He doesn't stay quiet. Verse 16 says Paul's nephew, his sister's son, went into the barracks and told Paul. Nothing in the text says he left Jerusalem. He walked toward the trouble and spoke up.

Not quite, friend. Paul doesn't go to the commander himself. In verse 17 he calls one of the centurions and says, "Take this young man to the commander; he has something to tell him." Paul sends his nephew along with a centurion instead.
Right. Paul doesn't go himself. He calls one of the centurions in verse 17 and asks him to take the young man to the commander. The nephew carries the news in.
Yes, baker. In verse 20 the nephew tells the commander the Jews will ask him to bring Paul to the Sanhedrin tomorrow. The commander hears about it from the nephew. That's a head start.
Next week is too far off. In verse 20 the nephew says the Jews will ask for Paul to be brought to the Sanhedrin tomorrow. That doesn't leave much time. It's a good thing he spoke up when he did.
Tonight isn't the word. In verse 20 the nephew says the request will be to bring Paul to the Sanhedrin tomorrow. That still leaves the commander very little time. The word is tomorrow.

It's the other way around. In verse 21 the nephew says, "Do not let them persuade you…" He tells the commander more than forty men are waiting to ambush Paul. The nephew is warning him not to go along with it.

Yes, friend. The nephew says, "Do not let them persuade you, because more than forty men are waiting to ambush him." (Acts 23:21) He also says they've bound themselves with an oath not to eat or drink until they've killed Paul. He's pleading with the commander to say no.

explanations.answer: Don't tell anyone you reported this
explanations.explanation: That's right. In verse 22 the commander instructs the young man, “Do not tell anyone that you have reported this to me.” The text doesn't give his reason. It only gives the instruction.

explanations.answer: Come back if you hear anything more
explanations.explanation: That's not in the text. In verse 22 the commander dismisses the young man and says, "Do not tell anyone that you have reported this to me." The only instruction is to keep quiet. No invitation to come back is mentioned.

explanations.answer: Go warn Paul's friends in the city
explanations.explanation: The commander says nothing about warning anyone. Verse 22 has him instruct the young man, "Do not tell anyone that you have reported this to me." That's the opposite of spreading the word. The young man is told to keep it to himself.

Not even close, friend. In verse 23 the commander orders two hundred soldiers, seventy horsemen and two hundred spearmen. That's a lot of people to move one man. A handful of guards would've needed a very big hand.

Yes, baker. Verse 23 has the commander tell two centurions to prepare two hundred soldiers, seventy horsemen and two hundred spearmen. That's nowhere near a handful. Claudius Lysias, the commander, is taking no chances.
That's the spot. In verse 23 the commander says to go to Caesarea. Verse 24 says to take Paul safely to Governor Felix, and in verse 33 the horsemen deliver him to the governor in Caesarea.
Joppa isn't the destination. Verse 23 says the commander orders the escort to go to Caesarea. That's where Paul is taken to Governor Felix. Joppa never shows up in this passage.
Damascus isn't the place the commander names. Verse 23 says the escort goes to Caesarea. Damascus isn't mentioned in this passage at all.
Not in daylight, friend. Verse 23 has the commander say to go in the third hour of the night. That's a night departure, not a daytime one.
That's right. The commander says in verse 23 to go to Caesarea in the third hour of the night. That's a night departure, not a daylight one. Paul leaves under the stars, not in the middle of the day.
That's right. Verse 24 says to take Paul safely to Governor Felix. A governor is the Roman official in charge of the region. Felix is the man at the end of the road.
King Agrippa isn't the one. Verse 24 says Paul is taken safely to Governor Felix. A governor is the Roman official in charge of the region. Agrippa isn't named in this passage.
The emperor isn't the stop. Verse 24 says Paul is taken to Governor Felix. A governor is the Roman official in charge of the region. Paul gets sent to Felix, and that's where this passage ends.

explanations.answer: He had learned Paul was a Roman citizen
explanations.explanation: That's the reason in the letter. Verse 27 has Lysias write that he came with his troops to rescue Paul, for he had learned that Paul is a Roman citizen. Lysias is the commander's name. That's how he tells it to Felix.

explanations.answer: He had heard Paul was a known prophet
explanations.explanation: The letter says nothing like that. In verse 27 Lysias writes that he came with his troops to rescue Paul, for he had learned that Paul is a Roman citizen. Prophet isn't a word in the letter. Roman citizen is the reason he gives.

explanations.answer: He had been ordered by the governor
explanations.explanation: The letter doesn't mention an order from the governor. Verse 27 has Lysias writing to Governor Felix that he came with his troops to rescue Paul, for he had learned Paul is a Roman citizen. Felix is the one reading the letter. Citizenship is the reason on the page.

That's it, baker. Verse 29 has Lysias write that the accusation involved questions about their own law. He also writes that he found no charge worthy of death or imprisonment. That's what he tells Felix in the letter.
That's not what the letter says. In verse 29 Lysias writes that the accusation involved questions about their own law. Riots against Rome aren't mentioned. The charges were about their law.
Stealing isn't in the letter. In verse 29 Lysias says the accusation involved questions about their own law. Nothing about money or a treasury appears in what he writes. It was about their law.

It's the reverse, friend. In verse 29 Lysias writes that there was "…no charge worthy of death or imprisonment." He says that right after saying the accusation involved questions about their own law. That's the letter Felix reads.
Yes. Lysias writes in verse 29, "…there was no charge worthy of death or imprisonment." That's the letter Felix reads. Neither death nor prison fits what Lysias says he found.
Yes, baker. Verse 30 has Lysias write that he instructed Paul's accusers to present their case against him before Felix. He tells Felix that in the letter. The accusers have been told where to go.

This one's True. In verse 30 Lysias writes that he also instructed Paul's accusers to present their case against Paul before Felix. It's right there in the letter. The accusers are told to take it to the governor.

That's right, baker. Verse 32 says that the next day the soldiers returned to the barracks and let the horsemen go on with Paul. So the big crowd heads home, and the horsemen carry on with him. Then verse 33 says the horsemen arrived in Caesarea and presented Paul to the governor.
The spearmen aren't the ones named. Verse 32 says the soldiers returned to the barracks and let the horsemen go on with Paul. The text names the horsemen as the ones who go on with him.

The centurions aren't named for this part. Verse 32 says the soldiers returned to the barracks, and the horsemen went on with Paul. The text doesn't say what the two centurions did. The horsemen finish the ride.

That's the one, baker. Felix reads the whole letter and then asks one plain question: what province is Paul from? Short question, short answer: Cilicia (v34). Then he says, “I will hear your case when your accusers arrive.”

Galatia isn't what Felix hears. He reads the letter, asks what province Paul is from, and learns it's Cilicia (v34). Then he says, “I will hear your case when your accusers arrive.” Felix gets one answer, and it isn't Galatia.

Macedonia isn't the province here. Verse 34 says Felix asks what province Paul is from, and Cilicia is what he learns. Then he says, “I will hear your case when your accusers arrive.” Macedonia gets no mention in this passage.

explanations.answer: Hear his case when the accusers arrive
explanations.explanation: That's it. In verse 35 Felix says, "I will hear your case when your accusers arrive." Then he orders Paul kept under guard in Herod's Praetorium. The case has to wait for the accusers to show up.

explanations.answer: Send him back to Jerusalem right away
explanations.explanation: Felix doesn't send him back. In verse 35 he says, "I will hear your case when your accusers arrive." He orders Paul kept under guard in Herod's Praetorium. Paul stays in Caesarea.

explanations.answer: Set him free since there's no charge
explanations.explanation: Felix doesn't set him free. Verse 35 has him say, "I will hear your case when your accusers arrive." Then he orders Paul kept under guard in Herod's Praetorium. Lysias's letter says there was no charge worthy of death or imprisonment (Acts 23:29), but Felix still waits to hear from the accusers.
